title: Diversity and final circuits
summary: Shows how diversity is applied to final circuits: cooker circuits, space heating, stored and instantaneous water heating, with worked demand calculations.

sections.heading: Diversity
paragraphs: For economic and reliable design within thermal limits and admissible voltage drop, the maximum demand must be determined (BS 7671: Section 3; 311.1). Diversity may be taken into account when determining it.

IET On-Site Guide Table A1 gives guidance on diversity for individual (final) circuits. Table A2 gives guidance on diversity for the installation as a whole, used to find the maximum demand current and therefore the rating of the main protective device.
bullets: Table A2: whole installation, main protective device rating

sections.heading: Cooker circuits
paragraphs: A cooker has a high current load, so it has a dedicated cable with a single cooker outlet, supplied from its own protective device (typically rated at 32 A).

For an individual household, On-Site Guide Appendix A, Table A1 allows: the first 10 A, plus 30% of full load of connected cooking appliances in excess of 10 A, plus 5 A if a socket outlet is in the control unit.

Example 1: 2 ✕ 1.0 kW and 2 ✕ 2.0 kW hob plates, a 2.0 kW oven/grill and a 3.0 kW oven at 230 V total 11 kW, so the current is 11 ✕ 1,000 ÷ 230 = 47.83 A. The first 10 A at 100% is 10 A; the remaining 37.83 A at 30% is 11.35 A; total 21.35 A. With a socket outlet in the control unit the rating must be at least 26.35 A.
bullets: Allowance: first 10 A + 30% of the rest + 5 A for a socket
Example 1 result: 21.35 A (26.35 A with socket)

sections.heading: Space heating circuits
paragraphs: Space heaters transfer heat mainly by convection or radiation. No diversity is allowed in cable size or protective device calculations for space heating circuits, because these appliances draw their maximum rated current for sustained periods (On-Site Guide Appendix A, Table A2).

Storage heaters contain heat-retaining clay bricks charged overnight by a heating element, releasing heat during the day through combined convection and radiation. Each needs a separate circuit with its own protective device, and a switched fused outlet adjacent to the heater.
bullets: Convection: elements warm the air directly, or heat oil or another filler
Radiation: tungsten filaments in quartz envelopes in front of a reflector
Underfloor: loose-fit wiring or heating mats
Switched fused outlet adjacent to the heater for flex connection

sections.heading: Stored water heating
paragraphs: Water heaters are either stored hot water (thermostatically controlled) or instantaneous. In stored systems a heating element sits in a cylinder, and Regulation 554.2.1 requires a means to automatically prevent a dangerous rise in temperature.

Regulation 554.3.3 requires an immersion heater to be fed from its own circuit and connected by a switched/fused connection unit adjacent to the cylinder using heat resistant flex. No diversity is allowed, as they draw maximum current for sustained periods.
bullets: 554.3.3: own circuit, switched/fused connection unit, heat resistant flex
No diversity for thermostatically controlled water heaters

sections.heading: Instantaneous water heating
paragraphs: Instantaneous heaters heat water as it flows and hold none except in the heat exchanger coil. Examples are instantaneous showers and point of use (POU) water heaters. A shower is fed from its own circuit in the ccu, with a double-pole switch near the unit.

Table A2 allows: 100% of full load of the largest appliance, plus 100% of the second largest, plus 25% of the remaining appliances. Example 2: four 8 kW showers and one 3 kW heater at 230 V. 8 kW is 34.8 A and 3 kW is 13.04 A. Two showers at 100% give 34.8 A each, the other two at 25% give 8.7 A each and the heater at 25% gives 3.26 A, totalling 90.26 A.

quiz.q: Which On-Site Guide table covers diversity for individual final circuits?
quiz.why: Table A1 provides guidance on diversity for individual (final) circuits.

quiz.q: What is a cooker circuit typically protected by?
options: A device typically rated at 32 A
quiz.why: A cooker circuit is typically on its own protective device rated at 32 A.

quiz.q: In the cooker diversity allowance, what percentage of connected cooking load above the first 10 A is included?
quiz.why: The allowance is 30% of full load in excess of 10 A.

quiz.q: A 230 V cooker totals 11 kW. What is its maximum current?
After diversity, what is the assumed demand for the 47.83 A cooker (no socket outlet)?
How much extra is added to the cooker demand if the control unit has a socket outlet?
How much diversity is allowed for space heating circuits?
quiz.why: No diversity is allowed as they draw maximum current for sustained periods.

quiz.q: Which regulation requires an immersion heater to have its own circuit and a switched/fused connection unit?
What is the allowance for the remaining instantaneous water heaters beyond the two largest?
quiz.why: The remainder are taken at 25% of full load.

quiz.q: What is the current of an 8 kW shower at 230 V (as given in the example)?
What is the total diversified current for four 8 kW showers and one 3 kW heater at 230 V?

options: A double-pole switch near the unit

quiz.why: It requires a means to automatically prevent a dangerous rise in temperature.
